strengths: The core idea is compelling and well-motivated: tokenizing molecules at the level of synthesis-compatible building blocks (amide, Suzuki, Buchwald-Hartwig disconnections) rather than atoms aligns molecular representation with both functional semantics and automated block-based chemistry, and is a genuinely interesting angle on molecule-language modeling.

The synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer with functional-group compatibility checks (Appendix D.1) is a thoughtful piece of chemistry-aware systems design, and the fallback rule-based tokenizer for training-time coverage is reasonable.

The bilingual 'code-switched' architecture (GNN-encoded block embeddings inserted into a pretrained LLM with a unified CCE loss) is cleanly presented, and training details (two-stage pretraining, separated molecule/text heads, GNN pretrained with MolCLR) are documented in reasonable depth.
The synthetic data pipeline (activity-cliff-based optimization pairs, property-to-molecule generation, OPV tasks) is creative and the dataset statistics are extensively tabulated.
The 'fallen angels' case studies (Evobrutinib, TNG348) are a memorable and practically relevant demonstration scenario, and the multi-step iterative refinement framing is sensible.
weaknesses: Serious evaluation circularity: the oracle ensemble models used to judge property improvement in Table 1 and Figure 4 are the SAME models used to generate synthetic training labels (Appendix B.2.3). The model is effectively trained against the evaluators, so 'improvement' may largely reflect learning/optimizing oracle quirks rather than genuine property gains. This invalidates the central quantitative claims as stated.

No baselines whatsoever. There is no comparison against SMILES/SELFIES-based LLM optimization, DrugAssist, simple random building-block replacement, genetic algorithms, or even an oracle-free ablation. Without baselines it is impossible to attribute the observed improvements to the modular bilingual design rather than to any optimization against the oracles.

Dependence on imperfect oracles (ensemble AUCs of 0.75-0.99, DILI only 0.84) makes large property swings (e.g., DILI 82.7 -> 50.0, BBBP 100 -> 2.31 -> 100 in Figure 4) more plausibly oracle exploitation than real chemistry. No wet-lab or synthesis validation is provided despite the headline claim of 'guaranteed' synthesizability.

Biological activity/potency is never evaluated: modifying FDA-approved drugs by swapping building blocks may destroy target binding (e.g., the kinase-binding pharmacophore of imatinib), yet only ADMET oracles are checked. The claim of 'improving drugs' is therefore substantially over-stated.

Out-of-distribution handling is unclear: the final model uses a 1,000-block vocabulary, but the FDA test set contains 796 unseen blocks; the paper does not explain how the GNN computes embeddings for unseen blocks or how reliable the GNN embeddings are, making the OOD claim hard to assess.

The modest aggregate gains in Table 1 (e.g., AMES 59.5->54.0, PGP actually worsens 66.0->68.0) plus a single Wilcoxon test pool unclear how the multiple per-property evaluations are conducted; effect sizes are small relative to oracle noise.

Claims of 'critical chemical reasoning' are not substantiated by any reasoning benchmark or controlled evaluation; Algorithm 1 is a generic propose-and-evaluate loop whose stopping criterion ('no clear objective remains') is undefined.

Signs of carelessness: an unresolved cross-reference ('Appendix ??' on page 24), duplicated references ([17]/[18], [37]/[38], [50]/[51], [68]/[71], [69]/[70]), and inconsistent text (426/430 vs. 'almost half') reduce confidence in overall rigor.

Novelty positioning is somewhat overstated: fragment/motif-level tokenization and synthesis-aware representation learning are well explored (FARM, BRICS/functional-group BERTs, reaction-aware representation learning), and the paper does not empirically compare against these closely related approaches.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated direction: aligning molecular tokenization with functional building blocks and block-based chemistry is a sensible and timely idea, and the connection to automated synthesis platforms gives the work a clear practical narrative.

Substantial data-engineering effort: a large multi-source training corpus (SMolInstruct, Tulu-3, Mol-Instructions, plus large-scale synthetic instruction data) is assembled and documented, with reasonable detail on tokenizers, oracle construction, and training procedure in the appendices.

The synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer, which restricts disconnections to automated amide/Suzuki/Buchwald-Hartwig couplings while checking functional-group compatibility, is a thoughtful and chemically informed design choice.
The 'fallen angels' case studies (Evobrutinib, TNG348) are engaging and illustrate a plausible real-world use case for iterative multi-property molecule refinement.
weaknesses: No baselines or comparisons: the evaluation never compares mCLM against any alternative (SMILES/SELFIES-based LLMs such as MolT5 or LlaSMol, graph-based models, or even ablations swapping modular tokens for atom-level tokenization). The core claim—that building-block tokenization is better—cannot be supported without this comparison.

Potentially circular evaluation: the same ensemble oracle models (FARM/ChemBERTa-2/GNN, AUC 0.84–0.99) are used both to generate synthetic training labels and to 'evaluate' the generated molecules. Improvements measured by these same noisy, possibly out-of-distribution oracles (e.g., on FDA drugs the paper itself notes the model is OOD) do not demonstrate real molecular improvement. No experimental or independent validation is provided.

The headline claim that mCLM 'guarantees to generate efficiently synthesizable molecules' is never tested: no molecules are actually synthesized, no retrosynthesis tool validation is reported, and the guarantee only holds within a vocabulary of three coupling reactions and a small curated block set, which also heavily restricts the accessible chemical space.

The main quantitative result is a single table on 430 FDA drugs, where 426/430 contain blocks unseen in training. How the model represents or scores unseen blocks is not clearly explained, and one of six properties (PGP) actually worsens, yet framing as '5/6 improved' with a Wilcoxon test on oracle outputs overstates the strength of the evidence.

Novelty over prior work is limited: functional-group/fragment-level tokenization and hierarchical molecular representations already exist (e.g., FARM [68], which shares authors, functional-group BERTs, motif-based GNNs), and the architectural contribution (GNN embeddings injected into an existing LLM à la LLaVA) is standard.

The 'critical chemical reasoning' component is under-specified: Algorithm 1 amounts to iterate-and-re-evaluate with oracle feedback, and the qualitative examples in Figure 4 show trade-offs (e.g., DILI improvements at the cost of PGP/AMES/BBBP) that the paper acknowledges but does not resolve.

Polish issues: a broken cross-reference ('Appendix ??'), duplicated references ([17]/[18], [37]/[38], [69]/[70]), and inconsistent claims (e.g., 'at least 3 blocks' vs. '3 or more') reduce confidence in rigor.

Scope mismatch with title/abstract: the paper emphasizes 'function-infused' design, but all evaluated functions are coarse ADMET proxy classifiers; there is no evidence of reasoning about actual biological function, binding, or target activity.

strengths: The core idea is compelling and well-motivated: tokenizing molecules at the level of synthesis-compatible building blocks (rather than atoms or full SMILES strings) and co-training with natural language functional descriptions is a genuinely interesting rethinking of molecular representation for LLMs.

The synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer grounded in real automated chemistry (amide coupling, Suzuki-Miyaura, Buchwald-Hartwig) is a thoughtful design choice, and the fallback rule-based tokenizer with coverage checking is described clearly (Figure 3, Appendix D).

The data creation pipeline is extensive and well documented: large-scale synthetic instruction data from real property datasets, activity-cliff-based optimization pairs, and oracle labeling, with detailed dataset statistics in Tables 2-3 and a broad list of source datasets.
The 'fallen angels' case study (Evobrutinib, TNG348) is a novel and practically relevant evaluation framing that demonstrates iterative multi-property refinement.
Writing is generally clear, with a good overview of related work spanning SMILES-based, graph-based, functional-group, and multimodal approaches.
weaknesses: No baseline comparisons. The paper never compares mCLM against existing molecule optimization or generation methods (e.g., DrugAssist, MolT5, LlaSMol, REINVENT-style optimizers, or even a simple random block replacement baseline). Without baselines, it is impossible to judge whether the modular tokenization actually helps relative to simpler alternatives.

Circular evaluation: the downstream improvements (Table 1, Figure 4) are measured by the same oracle ensemble models whose synthetic labels were used in training data generation (Appendix A/B.2.3). The oracles have only moderate AUC (e.g., DILI 0.84, GNN as low as 0.75), so a few-point average improvement on FDA drugs may partly reflect exploitation of oracle biases rather than genuine chemical improvement. No independent validation (e.g., wet-lab synthesis of even one proposed molecule, docking, or expert chemistry review) is provided.

The main results are thin: a single table of average property shifts on 430 FDA drugs, one 3-iteration case study on two molecules, and a frequency analysis of block modifications. Key generation-quality metrics expected in this field are missing: validity rate, novelty, diversity, uniqueness, and quantitative synthesizability verification of generated molecules (the synthesizability guarantee is asserted by construction but never actually verified, e.g., with a retrosynthesis tool or the actual synthesis platform).

Out-of-distribution handling is unclear: 426/430 test molecules contain blocks unseen in the 1000-block training vocabulary, yet the paper does not explain how OOV blocks are encoded at inference (fallback SMILES? nearest-neighbor retrieval?), nor does it quantify the effect of vocabulary size beyond brief dataset filtering notes. No ablation isolates the contribution of the synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer vs. the rule-based tokenizer, the bilingual function descriptions, or the GNN embeddings.

The 'reasoning' contribution (Section 2.5, Algorithm 1) is essentially iterative propose-and-evaluate with an oracle in the loop; there is no rigorous evaluation of chemical reasoning quality (e.g., benchmarks like MolCap-Arena or human evaluation of rationale text), and the loop depends on oracle scores whose reliability is limited.

Statistical reporting is weak: only 'p < 0.05 by Wilcoxon test' is claimed for 430 paired comparisons with no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or correction for the fact that PGP actually degraded (66.0 to 68.0), which is glossed over in the abstract's '5 out of 6' framing.

Some technical details are hand-wavy or contain errors (e.g., a broken appendix reference 'Appendix ??', 'TNG248' vs 'TNG348' inconsistency, duplicated near-identical references [17]/[18], [37]/[38], [50]/[51], [68]/[71]), and Figures 1-2 are dense and hard to parse; the model architecture details (embedding dim, adapter design) are buried in the appendix.

Scope of claims exceeds evidence: the abstract claims mCLM 'guarantees to generate efficiently synthesizable molecules' and 'reasons on multiple functions,' but the evidence is oracle-score-based property shifts without experimental synthesis, activity, or toxicity confirmation.

strengths: The core idea is compelling and well-motivated: tokenizing molecules at the level of synthesis-guaranteed building blocks (compatible with automated amide, Suzuki-Miyaura, and Buchwald-Hartwig couplings) creates a principled link between generation and automated lab synthesis, analogous to amino-acid-level tokenization in protein LLMs.

The synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer with functional-group conflict checks is a concrete, chemically-informed contribution, and the verified synthesizability results are strong: 100% validity and 98.2% retrosynthetic (Allchemy) success, exceeding even FDA-approved drugs.

Comprehensive experimental apparatus: 36M instruction examples, extensive appendices on data construction, oracle ensembles, tokenizer details, and training procedure; reproducibility statement and commitment to release code/data/models.

Baselines include strong recent text-based molecule editors (MoleculeSTM, FineMolTex, LDMol) and frontier LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-H), and out-of-distribution tests (122/430 drugs with unseen blocks) demonstrate some generalization.

The 'fallen angels' case study (rescuing Evobrutinib and TNG348) and the identification of functionally-important blocks (e.g., recapitulating the amphotericin B toxicity fix from Maji et al. 2023) are illustrative, high-value demonstrations.
weaknesses: Serious evaluation circularity: the ensemble oracles (FARM, ChemBERTa-2, GNN on the same six TDC ADMET tasks, Table 7) are used to generate training and finetuning labels (Appendix D.2.3, C.1), and the headline property improvements in Tables 1 and 4 are measured by (presumably) these same oracles. The model may largely exploit oracle biases on the training distribution rather than genuinely improving molecular functions; oracle AUCs (e.g., DILI 0.84) also limit the meaningfulness of predicted property changes. Independent validation (e.g., held-out experimental data, external oracles, or at least oracle-ensembles disjoint from training labels) is absent.

No wet-lab or even computational validation of biological function beyond oracle scores; the abstract's claims about 'significantly improving chemical functions critical to determining drug potentials' are stronger than the evidence supports.

Comparisons to LLM baselines are not fully controlled: mCLM is explicitly finetuned on 100k examples per property of oracle-labeled molecule-optimization data, while GPT-4o/GPT-5/Gemini/Claude presumably receive prompting only; a fair comparison would fine-tune open baselines or prompt-optimizer the closed ones equivalently.

Limited chemical coverage: the synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer covers only 26.7% of compounds and the deployed vocabulary is 1,000 blocks; most test drugs contain unseen blocks, so the 'guarantee' applies only to a narrow space, and the guaranteed-vs-actual synthesis of the proposed modified molecules on a real robotic platform is not demonstrated.

Small evaluation sets: 122 molecules for the main table, 200 randomly sampled molecules per model for the expensive Allchemy assessment; no error bars, significance tests, or diversity/novelty metrics (e.g., Tanimoto to parent drugs) are reported.

The 'critical chemical reasoning' (Section 2.3, Algorithm 1) is essentially a simple iterative property-improvement loop using oracle feedback, not the 'System 2' reasoning the introduction advertises; the mechanism is underspecified (how modifications are proposed, how many iterations, selection criteria).

Potential for oracle-gaming in generation is not analyzed: a generative model finetuned on oracle labels could produce molecules that score well on predicted properties while being pharmacologically implausible; adversarial/oracle-robustness checks would strengthen the claims.

strengths: The core idea of synthesis-guaranteed tokenization—restricting molecular tokens to building blocks compatible with a small set of automated reactions (amide coupling, Suzuki–Miyaura, Buchwald–Hartwig)—is a genuinely interesting and practically motivated contribution that directly links generation to physical-world feasibility.

The evaluation goes beyond cheap heuristics: in addition to SA scores, the authors use the Allchemy retrosynthesis engine to verify makeability of 200 sampled molecules per model, which is a more rigorous synthesizability assessment than is common in this literature.

Comparison against a wide and current set of baselines (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-Haiku, MoleculeSTM, FineMolTex, LDMol) and extensive appendix documentation of data generation (36M instructions), training procedure, and tokenizer rules support reproducibility.

The 'fallen angels' case study and the identification of functionally-important building blocks (e.g., the DILI modification resembling Maji et al. 2023) are engaging demonstrations of potential scientific utility.
weaknesses: Serious circularity in the central evaluation: the model is trained on ~12M 'Synthetic Oracle Data' labels generated by the ensemble oracle models (Table 5), and then evaluated on improvements in the very same six oracle-defined properties (AMES, BBBP, CYP3A4, DILI, HIA, PGP) on the same oracle models. The headline '15.0% avg improvement' therefore largely measures fit to the training signal, while baselines (GPT-5, Claude, MoleculeSTM, etc.) were never trained on these oracle labels. This makes the property-improvement comparison fundamentally unfair and undermines the paper's main claim.

The comparison on synthesizability is also confounded: mCLM is hard-constrained to a 582-block synthesis-guaranteed vocabulary, while all baselines generate freely. That mCLM achieves 100% validity and high synthesizability is close to guaranteed by construction, so Table 2's advantage is not an empirical finding about the model but a property of the output constraint.

No ablations are provided to justify the architectural choices: no comparison of building-block tokenization vs. BPE on SMILES or atom-level tokenization under matched data and compute; no ablation of the GNN encoder, the bilingual/code-switched training data, or the reasoning loop. The claim that modular tokenization (rather than just constrained decoding) drives the gains is not isolated.

Small and narrow evaluation: the main experiment uses only 122 FDA drugs and 6 ADMET tasks; no statistical significance, variance, or confidence intervals are reported, and with such small samples differences like 2.45% vs 1.64% between baselines are likely noise. No wet-lab or experimental validation is presented despite repeated claims about 'guarantees' in the physical world—oracle probability improvements are not evidence of real molecular function.

The synthesis guarantee is much weaker than advertised: the strictest tokenizer covers only 26.7% of the corpus, a rule-based fallback tokenizer is used for the rest, and the vocabulary is limited to 1,000 blocks—yet the abstract and introduction make broad claims ('guarantees automated synthesizability', 'makeable molecules') that the evidence does not support at this coverage.

The 'bilingual functional understanding from literature' aspect—the most novel-sounding part—is essentially unvalidated: no experiments demonstrate that mCLM's knowledge of function descriptions in natural language (rather than oracle-labeled property data) contributes to its performance.

The multi-step reasoning evaluation (Section 3.4) is anecdotal, involving only two molecules, with a qualitative MoleculeSTM comparison relegated to the appendix; claims about 'deliberate reasoning' and self-improvement are not backed by systematic evidence.

Novelty positioning is somewhat overstated: fragment/motif-level tokenization and fragment-aware molecular LLMs already exist (e.g., Fu et al. 2025, FARM, motif-based GNNs, MolCA-family models), and the incremental contribution—restricting disconnections to three automated reaction types—is narrower than the framing suggests.

Writing quality issues: several references are duplicated with inconsistent details (Li et al. 2015a/b, Blair et al. 2022a/b, Ertl 2009 twice), citations appear in the reference list without matching text (e.g., He et al. 2015, Zipf 1936, Buehler & Buehler 2024), and the stated 'Appendix A.3' comparison and 'Algorithm 1' references are loosely organized, suggesting insufficient polish.

strengths: The core idea is novel and well-motivated: tokenizing molecules at the level of synthesis-friendly building blocks (rather than atoms/SMILES characters) connects molecular generative modeling to real-world automated block chemistry, addressing a genuine gap between in silico generation and physical synthesizability.

The synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer is a principled contribution: disconnection rules tied to amide coupling, Suzuki-Miyaura, and Buchwald-Hartwig reactions, with functional-group compatibility checks, give a priori rather than post hoc synthesizability guarantees.

Evaluation is broader than typical molecule-generation papers: beyond oracle ADMET properties (Table 1), the paper reports validity, SA scores, and an expensive independent retrosynthesis check (Allchemy, Table 2), plus out-of-distribution testing (Appendix A.2) and a comparison of the 'fallen angels' case study against a baseline (Appendix A.3).

Comparison against strong and current baselines including GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-Haiku, MoleculeSTM, FineMolTex, and LDMol, with baselines allowed unconstrained generation, strengthens the headline result.

The construction of a large training corpus (36M instructions, 8M molecules, detailed dataset statistics in Appendices C-G) and a stated commitment to releasing code, data, and models supports reproducibility and follow-on work.
The library-design analysis (Section 3.3) and agreement with a human-discovered modification (Maji et al. 2023) provide some external scientific validation.
weaknesses: Potential circularity between training data and evaluation: the ADMET oracle ensemble (Appendix D.2.3, Table 7) is used to generate synthetic training labels, and oracles trained on the same TDC tasks appear to serve as the evaluation metric (Section 3.1). If the evaluation and training oracles share training data/architecture, mCLM's large property improvements (e.g., BBBP 85.2) may partly reflect optimization against the oracles rather than genuine property gains. The paper should clarify the separation between training oracles and evaluation oracles and ideally use truly held-out experimental endpoints.

Small and narrow primary evaluation set: the main result uses only 122 synthesis-guaranteed FDA drugs, and no statistical significance analysis (e.g., confidence intervals or paired tests across the 122 modifications) is provided, despite the margin over the best baseline (15.0% vs 6.98%) resting on aggregated average improvements.

The claim of 'guaranteed' synthesizability is partly by construction (molecules are assembled from pre-verified blocks with 2n-3 steps), so comparing SA scores against unconstrained baselines somewhat conflates a design constraint with learned capability; the more informative comparison would be mCLM evaluated with synthesis constraints removed versus baselines.

Generalization to unseen blocks (120/122 drugs contain out-of-vocabulary blocks) is demonstrated empirically but not analyzed; the mechanism by which GNN-derived features generalize to unseen blocks, and how vocabulary size (1,000 blocks) limits the accessible chemical space, deserves deeper discussion and ablation.

The 'iterative self-improvement / critical reasoning' component (Section 2.3, Algorithm 1) is largely an outer optimization loop using oracle feedback, not an internal reasoning capability of the model; the framing overstates this, and ablations isolating the contribution of the iterative loop versus single-shot generation are missing.

Several presentation issues: inconsistent reporting (e.g., BBBP source cited differently in Appendices G, oracle selection criteria AUC > 0.80 while some ensemble tasks score below), heavy reliance on appendix material for key details, and some sweeping claims (e.g., 'guarantees' synthesis, 'first attempt') that exceed what is shown.

The impact of the rule-based fallback tokenizer (used for ~73% of the corpus) on the synthesis guarantee is underexplored; it is unclear how much of the training distribution actually supports the guarantee at inference time.

strengths: The core idea of tokenizing molecules at the level of synthesis-friendly, function-infused building blocks (rather than atoms) is well-motivated and grounded in a real physical constraint (automated block chemistry with Suzuki/Buchwald-Hartwig/amide couplings), giving a genuine bridge between generative models and lab synthesizability.

The bilingual molecule-text formulation with GNN-encoded blocks inserted into a pretrained LLM backbone (Qwen2.5-3B) is a clean, principled architecture, and the paper provides honest ablations (No GNN, No Synth. Tokenizer, Llama backbone) showing that both the GNN encoding and the synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer matter substantially.

Evaluation goes beyond superficial metrics: validity, SA score, and rigorous retrosynthetic validation via Allchemy (200 sampled molecules per model on a supercomputing cluster), plus makeability as a combined metric. Comparisons against a broad set of baselines including GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-H, MoleculeSTM, FineMolTex, LDMol, HierVAE, and DGAE.

Comprehensive appendix covering data construction (36M instructions, activity-cliff based optimization data), oracle ensemble details with reported AUCs, tokenizer mechanics with lossless reconstruction examples, and out-of-distribution testing on 430 FDA drugs.
The 'fallen angels' case study and the block-preference analysis (Figure 5, echoing the amphotericin B result from Maji et al.) are compelling demonstrations of practical relevance.
weaknesses: Potential circularity between training and evaluation: the same oracle ensemble (FARM/ChemBERTa-2/GNN, AUC 0.84-0.99) is used both to generate ~12M synthetic training labels (Appendix D.2.3) and to evaluate the property improvements in Tables 1 and 4. Optimizing against the evaluation oracle inflates the reported gains; the paper would benefit from evaluation on held-out experimental data or oracles disjoint from training labels.

Scale and diversity of the demonstrated capability is limited: the main result covers only 122 synthesis-guaranteed FDA drugs with an output vocabulary confined to 582 blocks, and the training vocabulary is restricted to 1,000 blocks. Claims of generalization to 'unseen blocks' are supported but the evidence base is narrow.

Some reported improvements look suspiciously large relative to the oracle quality (e.g., BBBP 61.4 -> 85.2 from single-block modifications), which may reflect oracle exploitation rather than genuine pharmacological improvement; no statistical significance testing, uncertainty quantification, or multiple-sample-per-drug analysis is reported.

The 'fallen angels' reasoning case study involves only two molecules and is largely qualitative; the multi-step 'critical reasoning' loop (Algorithm 1) has no systematic benchmark quantifying its benefit over single-step editing.

The synthesis guarantee is strong but restrictive: only three reaction types are supported, and the strict tokenizer covers only 26.7% of compounds in the corpus. The claim of a 'direct link between digital and physical worlds' is not yet validated by any actual laboratory synthesis of proposed molecules.

Writing is often overreaching and promotional (e.g., 'better, faster, stronger', 'guarantees to generate efficiently synthesizable molecules', broad claims about democratizing drug discovery), and positioning relative to Group-SELFIES, SAFE, and Reasyn, while discussed, does not include direct experimental comparison with these most-related tokenization schemes.

Comparisons with frontier LLM baselines (GPT-5, Gemini, Claude) lack details on prompting, sampling temperature, number of retries, and self-consistency settings, making it hard to verify that baselines were given a fair chance (GPT-5 scoring negative improvement while Gemini achieves 6.98% suggests high prompt sensitivity).

strengths: The core idea—tokenizing molecules at the level of synthesis-guaranteed building blocks (amide, Suzuki, Buchwald-Hartwig couplings) rather than atoms—is well-motivated and builds naturally on the block-chemistry literature (Burke's MIDA chemistry, automated synthesis platforms). It provides a principled link between generation and physical synthesizability.

The synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer with coverage checks and a fallback rule-based tokenizer is carefully engineered, with lossless reconstruction examples and modularity for adding new reactions; tokenizer details and placeholder-based reconstruction are well documented in Appendix F.

Broad empirical evaluation: comparisons against 7+ baselines including recent commercial LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-Haiku), fine-tuned molecule-text models (MoleculeSTM, FineMolTex, LDMol), and structure-based generators (HierVAE, DGAE), plus rigorous external retrosynthesis validation via Allchemy rather than relying solely on heuristic SA scores.

Reasonable ablation studies (No GNN, No Synth. Tokenizer, Llama vs. Qwen backbone), and an attempt at out-of-distribution evaluation (122 synthesis-guaranteed FDA drugs with 153 unseen blocks; 430-drug expanded test).
Significant infrastructure contribution: a large dataset (36M instructions, 800k blocks, 200k synthesis-guaranteed) with stated plans for release.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation circularity: the training data includes 'Synthetic Oracle Data' generated by ensemble ADMET oracles (Appendix D.2.3) built on the very same six TDC tasks (AMES, BBBP, CYP3A4, DILI, HIA, PGP) that are then used as the headline evaluation metrics (Tables 1, 4, 8, 11). A model fine-tuned on labels from these oracles can inflate oracle scores without producing genuinely better molecules; no independent experimental or clinically-derived validation of the property improvements is provided. This undermines the central claim of 'significantly improving chemical functions.'

The main property-improvement evaluation is small and statistically fragile: 122 molecules (430 in the appendix), 200 molecules sampled for Allchemy analysis, single-point averages with no variance, confidence intervals, significance tests, or number of samples per drug; 'Avg. Improvement' percentages are reported without any error analysis.

Unfair baseline conditions: commercial LLMs (GPT-5, Gemini, Claude) are prompted only, while mCLM is a 3B model fully fine-tuned on ~1M task-specific examples (including 100k examples per property on the exact evaluation properties). A fine-tuned SMILES-based LLM baseline at matched compute/data would be a much more meaningful comparison; the No-GNN ablation partially addresses this but conflates tokenizer and GNN changes.

The 'synthesizability guarantee' is overstated: guarantees hold only if all building blocks are commercially available and the automated platform handles all proposed assemblies; no wet-lab synthesis of any mCLM-generated molecule is demonstrated, and the claim that Allchemy agreement validates 'makeability' is weakened by the authors' own admission that Allchemy saturates on this distribution (>98% for FDA drugs and baselines).

Novelty positioning is incomplete: fragment/motif-based tokenization (Group-SELFIES, BRICS, MolBert, FARM, SAFE, HiGen, MolXPT, Reasyn) is acknowledged but the paper does not clearly quantify what is new beyond restricting disconnections to three reaction types; the 'No Synth. Tokenizer' ablation uses BRICS rather than, e.g., Group-SELFIES, which would be the more direct competitor.

Multi-step 'reasoning' (Section 2.3, Algorithm 1) is essentially greedy one-property-at-a-time oracle-guided editing; the 'fallen angels' case study (2 molecules) is anecdotal, and the paper itself concedes other properties may be compromised—no systematic multi-objective evaluation (e.g., Pareto analysis) is provided.

Writing is promotional and overclaims ('rescue drug candidates that failed late in clinical trials', 'guarantees to generate efficiently synthesizable molecules', 'better, faster, stronger'), with several tables containing inconsistent/unexplained values (e.g., Table 1 HIA for LDMol at 99.0 vs. FDA 98.96 counted as worse; BBBP jump to 85.2 with no plausibility discussion).

Reproducibility is promised ('will be released upon publication') but code/data are not available at review time, and several key details (how exactly outputs are decoded to molecules, inference-time vocabulary confinement mechanics, similarity/constraint checks) are underspecified.

strengths: The core idea of tokenizing molecules at the level of synthesis-guaranteed functional building blocks (rather than atoms or generic motifs) is novel, well-motivated, and naturally connects molecular generation to automated block chemistry platforms, guaranteeing synthesizability a priori rather than as a post-hoc filter.

The synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer is thoughtfully designed: disconnection rules tied to three automation-compatible reactions, functional-group conflict checks, placeholder-atom encoding enabling lossless reconstruction, and modularity for adding new reactions. Detailed tokenizer mechanics are documented in Appendix F.

Evaluation is unusually broad: property improvements on FDA drugs (both synthesis-guaranteed and non-guaranteed distributions), rigorous retrosynthetic assessment via Allchemy on a supercomputing cluster (rather than only SA scores), comparisons against 7+ strong baselines including frontier LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-3.5-H) and structure-based baselines (HierVAE, DGAE), plus QM9 synthesizability comparison.
The paper includes substantive ablations: No-GNN and No-Synth-Tokenizer variants degrade performance significantly, and a backbone comparison (Qwen-2.5 vs Llama-3.2) supports architectural choices.

Interesting qualitative demonstrations: the 'fallen angel' case studies (Evobrutinib, TNG348) with iterative multi-step reasoning, and the observation that mCLM-preferred DILI modifications resemble a recently published human-discovered amphotericin B modification (Maji et al., 2023), which lends external validity.

A reproducibility statement and detailed appendices (data mixture, training procedure, oracle construction, tokenizer rules) suggest the work will be reproducible; the authors commit to releasing data and code.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in evaluation: oracle ensemble models (built from TDC datasets) are used both to generate synthetic training labels (Appendix D.2.3: 12M+ 'Synthetic Oracle Data' samples) and as the evaluation metric. Property 'improvements' (e.g., BBBP 61.4 -> 85.2) may partly reflect overfitting to or exploiting the oracles (Goodharting), which undermines confidence that real pharmacological functions improved. The paper does not adequately address this risk.

Reported property values appear to be oracle-derived probabilities/scores, not experimental measurements. There is no wet-lab synthesis or assay validation of any proposed molecule, so central claims about 'functional' molecules rest entirely on computational proxies.

Synthetic accessibility gains over baselines may partly reflect vocabulary constraints rather than learned synthesizability: mCLM can only emit 582 synthesis-guaranteed blocks in the main experiment while baselines generate freely, making the SA/makeability comparison somewhat structurally advantaged.

The strict synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer covers only ~26.7% of the corpus, so most training molecules use the fallback rule-based tokenizer; the practical chemical space of the synthesis-guaranteed vocabulary (3 reaction types) is narrow and may not generalize to many drug-like chemotypes.

The multi-function reasoning claims ('iteratively self-improve', 'rescue fallen angels') are demonstrated on only two molecules, acknowledged by the authors to possibly compromise other properties; statistical significance, variance across seeds/samples, and quantitative multi-objective trade-off analysis are not reported for the main Table 1 results.

Coverage of out-of-vocabulary blocks relies on GNN embeddings computed at inference, but the vocabulary is limited to the top-1000 blocks during training; scaling behavior and quality of embeddings for the full 800k-block vocabulary remain untested, leaving open questions about whether the claimed generalization extends beyond curated test settings.
